intro: The Third Ballade grows from a quietly exchanging pair of phrases into a much more forceful return. Martha Goldstein’s performance lets you follow the family resemblance between the singing opening, the rocking second idea and the later rapid passagework.
question: Can you recognise the opening when it returns with more weight?

sections.label: B′ · Second idea transformed
sections.mNote: the rocking idea returns in a darker harmonic setting

sections.label: A′ · Opening enlarged
sections.mNote: the opening returns with stronger bass and fuller chords

cues.title: A conversation before motion
cues.text: The opening’s short phrases answer one another across the keyboard. Listen for that exchange before the more continuous rocking and flowing material arrives: this is the theme whose return will close the larger arch.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the opening theme and its returning role: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

cues.title: Follow the answering voice
cues.text: Rather than hearing only a tune above accompaniment, try following whichever register carries the next answering phrase. The opening’s dialogue can survive as its chords and decorations become fuller.
cues.evidence: General listening invitation grounded in the opening’s dialogue; no exact voice entrance is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening gains weight
cues.text: Goldstein’s opening span expands well beyond its quiet beginning. Listen to the supporting chords as well as the melody: a change in the weight of accompaniment can make a returning phrase feel newly emphatic.
cues.evidence: Report shows the opening rising from approximately −42 to −34 dB at 0:05–0:20 to −19 to −16 dB at 0:50–1:05. This anchors a broad dynamic contrast, not a touch judgement.

cues.title: A summer at Nohant
cues.text: Chopin composed the Third Ballade in 1841, during a summer with George Sand at Nohant. The domestic circumstances belong to the work’s history; they do not supply a literal narrative for its musical themes.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski’s account of the work’s composition: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

cues.title: A rocking second idea
cues.text: The second principal idea grows from a repeated-note gesture into a rocking melody. Its syncopations make accents hover against the metre. Keep its rhythmic profile in mind for the more turbulent transformation later.
cues.evidence: Approximate beginning at the strongest novelty peak, 2:08, after very quiet windows at 1:55–2:00. The second theme’s syncopation is described by https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Accent against accompaniment
cues.text: In the second-theme region, compare the melodic accents with the more regular motion below them. Syncopation means that the points of emphasis do not all coincide with the expected strong beats.
cues.evidence: Explanation of the second theme’s documented syncopated construction; no beat-level alignment claimed. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

cues.title: A pupil’s dedication
cues.text: The score is dedicated to Pauline de Noailles, one of Chopin’s pupils. Such dedications connect these concert works with the Parisian teaching and private music-making through which much of his piano music circulated.
cues.evidence: Dedicatee and pupil relationship in Tomaszewski’s work commentary: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

cues.title: A more continuous surface
cues.text: The middle of the arch offers a more flowing idea. Listen for the distinction between a melody supported by chords and a line carried within continuous figuration; both can be songful, but they distribute attention differently.
cues.evidence: Approximate episode opening at 4:04, a report boundary preceding a rise in activity. Three thematic ideas and the later return of the third are described by https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No fixed fairy tale
cues.text: The Ballade has been linked to poems about water spirits, but those associations are interpretations, not an authorised programme. Recognising how its themes return offers firmer guidance than assigning each passage a character or scene.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski discusses Undine and Lorelei associations as hypotheses: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

cues.title: The second idea darkens
cues.text: The rocking idea returns in a more restless setting. Its repeated-note shape remains a thread to follow while fuller figuration and a darker tonal region turn a familiar theme into a source of tension.
cues.evidence: Approximate return near report boundary 5:06; transformation through C-sharp minor is described in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Not a chroma-based key claim.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognition through changed texture
cues.text: As the later span gathers force, try to recognise a melodic or rhythmic outline rather than an identical sonority. Chopin’s return can preserve the theme while replacing its original light accompaniment with much denser writing.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation to thematic transformation in the arch; no exact entrance or chord identification.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening returns enlarged
cues.text: The opening theme returns near the climax, now with fuller chords and a more emphatic bass. It is not simply the first page played again: the intervening movement changes the scale of its statement.
cues.evidence: Approximate return at 6:18; report has sustained high level around 6:30–6:55. Return in A-flat and fuller writing: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The closing surge
cues.text: The final expansion condenses the piece’s flowing energy into a decisive close. Listen for the contrast between rapid movement and the final chords, which stop that motion rather than letting it fade indefinitely.
cues.evidence: Approximate coda at report boundary 7:06; late sounding windows at 7:10–7:20 give way to near silence at 7:25. Closing figuration and four chords: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Repose prepares a new rhythmic idea
transitions.how: The opening’s exchange of phrases settles before a repeated-note gesture introduces the rocking second idea. The new melody is distinguished by its syncopated emphasis, not by a wholly unrelated metre. A very quiet space in this performance makes the change of rhythmic character especially legible.
transitions.evidence: Strongest boundary at 2:08 follows low levels at 1:55–2:00; thematic contrast: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

transitions.title: Rocking becomes continuous figuration
transitions.how: A more continuously moving figure takes the foreground after the rocking melody. Instead of a sharply accented melodic profile supported by accompaniment, the hands share a flowing texture. This central episode gives the later returns something more active to absorb.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 4:04 supports an approximate placement. Third idea and its flowing character: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110

transitions.title: A familiar rhythm returns in changed surroundings
transitions.how: The repeated-note identity of the second idea returns, but its darker harmonic setting and fuller figuration change its effect. Listen for the retained rhythm inside the new activity. The return begins the other half of the arch rather than supplying an exact repeat of the earlier episode.
transitions.evidence: Approximate report boundary 5:06; formal order and C-sharp-minor transformation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

transitions.title: The opening becomes the climactic theme
transitions.how: The later development gathers enough force to bring back the opening idea in a larger texture. Fuller chords and bass support make the earlier dialogue sound public and emphatic. The thematic return and recovery of A♭ major work together: recognition also supplies tonal orientation.
transitions.evidence: Report boundary 6:18 before the late sustained crest; tonal return and fuller writing: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

transitions.title: The return feeds a final flourish
transitions.how: The enlarged opening does not finish with the restrained exchange heard at the start. Flowing passagework carries its energy into the coda, where the remaining motion is brought to a close by emphatic chords. Texture, rather than the introduction of another principal theme, marks the final expansion.
transitions.evidence: Estimated coda at the 7:06 boundary; late activity and terminal decline in the report. Closing design: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
